screens.title: Redis Backups, Restores, and High Availability
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we will make your Redis deployments resilient through practical backup, restore, and high availability patterns. You will learn how to produce consistent backups from both snapshot (RDB) and append-only (AOF) persistence, how to verify and restore those backups, and why each persistence mode matters for recovery timelines. We will then introduce Redis Sentinel and explain how it monitors Redis instances, elects leaders during failures, and provides a configuration endpoint clients can query so they don't hardcode master addresses. I will also briefly compare Sentinel with Redis Cluster to clarify when you need sharding versus when you need failover only. A concrete example you will use in the hands-on activity is creating an RDB snapshot with BGSAVE, copying the resulting dump file off-server, simulating data loss, and restoring from that file. A common misconception is thinking backups alone prevent downtime; they protect data but not availability. Sentinel addresses availability by promoting replicas automatically. By the end of this chapter you will have clear, repeatable steps to back up and restore, a working mental model for Sentinel failover, and guidance on when to consider the added complexity of a Redis Cluster.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Redis Backups & HA
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Redis Backups, Restores, and High Availability

Learn repeatable, production-safe steps to back up Redis data with RDB and AOF, restore reliably, and keep services running using Redis Sentinel. We also introduce when Redis Cluster is appropriate.

In this lesson
  • Backups: Create safe copies of dump.rdb and appendonly.aof with BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF.
  • Restores: Stop Redis, replace persistence files, and restart to recover state.
  • HA with Sentinel: Monitor, notify, promote replicas, and provide master info to clients.
Concept Map
RDB / AOF
Persistence files on disk used for backups and restores.
Sentinel
Monitors instances, triggers failover, serves master address to clients.
Coming up
Backups
Use BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF, then copy files off-server.
Restores
Stop Redis, replace files, restart to recover data.
HA
Sentinel automates failover; Cluster provides sharding and scale.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define the hands-on and conceptual skills you'll build. First, you will develop practical strategies for backing up Redis data using both RDB snapshots and the append-only AOF file. That means learning the commands to create consistent backups, when to compact AOF, and where to store files off-server. Second, you will perform restores from RDB and AOF files so you understand the exact stop, replace, and restart sequence and how to verify a successful recovery. Third, you will understand Redis Sentinel: how it monitors instances, sends notifications, and performs automatic failover when necessary. The narration will show how Sentinels agree by quorum and how they elect a leader for failover. Fourth, you will learn how to explain Sentinel’s role as a configuration provider so clients can discover the current master address instead of hardcoding it. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue you can use to remember the steps, and every objective links to a verified competency milestone you can test in a sandbox. Practicing these goals will prepare you to keep Redis data safe, to restore quickly when problems occur, and to reduce unplanned downtime through automated failover.

screens.title: Persistence Modes: RDB and AOF
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the two persistence modes available in Redis because your backup strategy depends on them. RDB produces point-in-time snapshots as a single binary file named dump. rdb; it is efficient for periodic, compressed backups and for fast startup because loading a single snapshot is quick. AOF records every write operation and can provide a more up-to-date recovery point, but AOF files are larger and require replay on restart. For a concrete example, imagine a shopping cart service: using RDB with regular snapshots gives you a reasonable recovery if you can tolerate up to a snapshot interval of data loss, while enabling AOF reduces that potential loss to the time between writes and the last AOF flush. A common misconception is that one persistence mode is always enough; many production deployments enable both to trade a quick restore with snapshots and a finer-grained recovery with AOF. When you plan backups, consider restore time, acceptable data-loss window, disk usage, and startup performance. As you work through the hands-on activity, pick the mode that matches your recovery point objective and validate it with a test restore so you can trust the recovery SLA.

keyIdea.title: RDB vs AOF
keyIdea.text: RDB snapshots are compact and fast to load; AOF provides finer recovery at cost of larger files and replay time.

content.html:
Core Concept › Persistence Modes

Definition & trade-offs

RDB: periodic snapshot file. AOF: append-only log of writes. Choose based on recovery point objectives and startup time.

RDB — snapshot
Compact file, faster load, coarser recovery window.
AOF — command log
Fine-grained recovery, larger files, replay time on startup.
Concrete example
Shopping cart scenario: RDB snapshots every minute may lose recent adds; enabling AOF reduces potential loss to seconds at the cost of larger disk and longer restarts.
Check your understanding
  • When does RDB give the fastest restart? When loading a single snapshot at server start.
  • Why might AOF slow restart? Because Redis replays many commands to rebuild dataset.
  • Misconception: enabling both guarantees zero data loss — not by itself; you still need appropriate fsync and backup scheduling.
Key Takeaway

Pick RDB for compact snapshots and AOF for fine-grained recovery; combine them for balanced safety and performance.

screens.title: Creating an RDB Backup
screens.narratorSegment: Backing up an RDB snapshot is a simple, repeatable process that you should automate. First, confirm RDB persistence is enabled in redis. conf via the save directives; these settings decide when Redis creates periodic snapshots. Second, trigger an immediate snapshot with BGSAVE so the server creates a fresh dump without blocking clients. Third, wait for the BGSAVE completion message or check the last save time, then locate the dump. rdb file in the configured dir and dbfilename locations. Fourth, copy that file to an off-server location such as cloud storage or a separate backup host, and add a timestamp to the filename to keep versions. For example, after running BGSAVE you might run a command to copy dump. rdb to /tmp/redis_backup/dump-2023-07-01. rdb. A common mistake is copying the file before BGSAVE finishes, which yields an old snapshot; always confirm completion. Another trap is keeping backups on the same disk — off-site copies are essential. As a practice, automate BGSAVE triggers and file transfer and make sure your restore process is tested periodically so backups are not just created, but also usable when you need them.

keyIdea.title: RDB backup checklist
keyIdea.text: Enable snapshots, run BGSAVE, confirm completion, and copy dump.rdb off-server with timestamps.

content.html:
Process Flow › RDB Backup
  1. Verify save directives: Ensure redis.conf has the desired snapshot intervals.
  2. Trigger snapshot: Run BGSAVE to create a background dump.
  3. Confirm completion: Check LASTSAVE or logs to ensure dump finished.
  4. Copy with timestamp: Move dump.rdb off-server for retention.
Pro tip: automate BGSAVE and the file copy so manual steps are not missed.
Terminal commands (example)
# Trigger a fresh snapshot in redis-cli
BGSAVE

# After completion, copy the file with a timestamp
cp /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb /tmp/redis_backup/dump-2023-07-01.rdb
Key Takeaway

Always confirm BGSAVE completion and copy dump.rdb to off-server storage with a timestamp.

screens.title: Restoring from an RDB Backup
screens.narratorSegment: Restoring from an RDB file is straightforward but must be done carefully to avoid corruption or partial restores. The safe sequence is: stop the Redis server cleanly so it does not overwrite or conflict with the file you will restore; place your validated dump. rdb into the Redis dir configured in redis. conf; then restart the Redis server so it will load the snapshot at startup. For example, after copying your backup dump into the configured directory, run the server start command and then verify keys using redis-cli GET or HGET. A common mistake is attempting to replace the file while Redis is running, which can cause the running process to overwrite the file or encounter inconsistent state. Another misconception is that restores are instant — loading a large snapshot can take time and you should monitor server logs for completion. Always practice the restore in a staging environment to confirm timelines and the correctness of your backup selection. Finally, consider locking or versioning the dir during restore so multiple processes do not interfere with the operation. Restoring from an RDB Backup means stop redis, replace dump.rdb in the configured dir, restart, and verify with commands in redis-cli.. In practical terms, stop redis, replace dump.rdb, and restart to recover state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Restore safety
keyIdea.text: Stop Redis, replace dump.rdb in the configured dir, restart, and verify with commands in redis-cli.

content.html:
Process Flow › RDB Restore

Step-by-step restore

  • Stop Redis: Ensure a clean shutdown to avoid write conflicts.
  • Place dump.rdb: Move your backup file into the configured dir.
  • Start Redis: The server will load the snapshot on startup.
  • Verify: Use redis-cli to check critical keys and data integrity.
Misconception: Replacing files while Redis runs is safe — it is not. Always stop first.
Example commands
# Stop Redis (systemd example)
systemctl stop redis

# Copy backup into Redis dir
cp /tmp/redis_backup/dump-2023-07-01.rdb /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb

# Start Redis
systemctl start redis

# Verify data
redis-cli GET user:1:name
Key Takeaway

Always stop before replacing persistence files and verify restored keys after restart.

screens.title: Creating and Compacting an AOF Backup
screens.narratorSegment: AOF backups require additional care because the file records every write and can grow quickly. First, enable AOF by setting appendonly yes in redis. conf and confirm the appendfilename and dir settings. Second, trigger BGREWRITEAOF to compact the AOF into a smaller, optimized file that removes redundant commands; BGREWRITEAOF runs in the background and produces a compacted appendonly. aof. Third, after BGREWRITEAOF completes, copy the resulting appendonly. aof to a safe off-server location, applying timestamps so you can choose the correct recovery point. A concrete example: after a large ingestion job, run BGREWRITEAOF then copy appendonly. aof to cloud storage. A common mistake is copying the AOF before compaction, which produces larger files and slower restores. Also avoid keeping backups on the same disk. Finally, remember that restoring from AOF involves replaying commands during startup, which can take additional time proportional to the file size; plan restore windows accordingly and test them in staging. Creating and Compacting an AOF Backup means enable appendonly, run bgrewriteaof to compact, and copy appendonly.aof off-server; expect longer replay time on restore.. In practical terms, enable aof, run bgrewriteaof, and copy the appendonly.aof file off-server.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AOF backup steps
keyIdea.text: Enable appendonly, run BGREWRITEAOF to compact, and copy appendonly.aof off-server; expect longer replay time on restore.

content.html:
Process Flow › AOF Backup

Why compact AOF?

AOF records every write. Over time this accumulates redundant operations. BGREWRITEAOF produces a compact file that reduces restore time and disk use.

Common-mistake
Copying the AOF before compaction creates unnecessarily large backups and slow replays.
Terminal example
# Trigger AOF rewrite
BGREWRITEAOF

# After rewrite, copy the file
cp /var/lib/redis/appendonly.aof /tmp/redis_backup/appendonly-2023-07-01.aof
Key Takeaway

Run BGREWRITEAOF to compact before copying and expect replay time during AOF restore.

screens.title: Restoring from an AOF Backup
screens.narratorSegment: Restoring from AOF differs from RDB because Redis will replay the logged operations to rebuild the dataset. The safe restore sequence is: stop the Redis server, place the appendonly. aof file into the configured dir with the correct appendfilename, and restart Redis so it can read and replay the commands. During restart Redis will process each entry; for large AOF files this can take time proportional to the command count. A concrete scenario: you compacted an AOF, copied it off-site, and now need to restore after data loss. You would stop Redis, replace appendonly. aof, restart, and then monitor logs for replay completion before sending production traffic. A misconception is thinking AOF restores are faster than RDB; in many cases a compacted AOF can be larger than RDB and will take longer because it has to execute commands. Always test your AOF restore process to understand time requirements and any command semantics that might change during replay. Restoring from an AOF Backup means aof replays commands during startup. expect longer startup times and test restores to measure them.. In practical terms, stop redis, place appendonly.aof, restart and let aof replay rebuild state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › AOF Restore

Restore steps

  1. Stop Redis cleanly.
  2. Copy appendonly.aof into Redis dir.
  3. Start Redis and wait for command replay to finish.
  4. Verify data integrity using client checks.
Misconception: AOF always restores faster than RDB — not necessarily; replay time can be significant.
Example commands
# Stop Redis
systemctl stop redis

# Replace the AOF file
cp /tmp/redis_backup/appendonly-2023-07-01.aof /var/lib/redis/appendonly.aof

# Start Redis
systemctl start redis

# Verify a sample key
redis-cli GET user:1:name
Key Takeaway

AOF restores replay all writes. Test replay time and plan maintenance windows accordingly.

screens.title: Redis Sentinel: Purpose and Core Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Redis Sentinel is a small distributed system that provides high availability for a Redis deployment. Its responsibilities are fourfold: continuous monitoring of master and replica instances, notification to operators or monitoring systems when anomalies are detected, automatic failover to promote a replica to master when a master is unavailable, and serving as a configuration provider that clients can query for the current master address. For example, if a master becomes unresponsive, Sentinels mark it subjectively down and then, through a quorum of Sentinels, mark it objectively down. Once the quorum agrees, they elect a leader Sentinel to orchestrate failover: choose the best replica, promote it, reconfigure remaining replicas to follow the new master, and inform clients. A common misconception is that Sentinel replaces backups: it does not. Sentinel reduces downtime by automating role changes but does not undo data loss that occurred before backups. Understanding Sentinel’s roles clarifies why production systems usually combine backups for data safety and Sentinel for availability. Redis Sentinel: Purpose and Core Functions means sentinel monitors, notifies, performs failover, and tells clients which node is master — but it is not a backup system.. In practical terms, monitoring, notification, automatic failover, and configuration provider.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Redis Sentinel

Core functions

  • Monitoring: Constant health checks on master and replicas.
  • Notification: Alert operators or systems when issues occur.
  • Automatic failover: Elect and promote a replica when master fails.
  • Configuration provider: Give clients the current master address.
Example: failover sequence
  1. Sentinel marks master as subjectively down.
  2. Quorum of Sentinels agree and mark it objectively down.
  3. Sentinels elect a leader to coordinate failover.
  4. Leader promotes the best replica and reconfigures others.
Key Takeaway

Use Sentinel to reduce downtime. Combine it with backups to protect both availability and data integrity.

screens.title: Sentinel Configuration and Quorum
screens.narratorSegment: A healthy Sentinel deployment uses multiple Sentinel processes on separate hosts and a quorum-based decision to avoid split-brain. The sentinel. conf includes a monitor line that names the master and sets the quorum number — for example, sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2 requires at least two Sentinels to agree a master is down before failover. Sentinels first detect outages subjectively; then when enough Sentinels report the same condition, the master becomes objectively down and a leader is elected to manage failover. Running at least three Sentinels ensures no single Sentinel can unilaterally decide failure and allows a majority to form. A common operational pitfall is collocating Sentinels with the master as they then risk being unavailable during the same outage; place Sentinels on separate hosts or availability zones. Another misconception is that a higher quorum is always safer; too high a quorum can prevent failover if Sentinels are temporarily partitioned. Balance quorum and placement for reliable failover. Practice reviewing sentinel. conf and simulating failover in a staging environment to validate your choices. keyIdea.text: Use at least three Sentinels on separate hosts and choose quorum to balance safety and availability; avoid collocating Sentinels with the master.

content.html:
Architecture › Sentinel Quorum
sentinel.conf example
# sentinel monitor    
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2

# common options
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000
sentinel parallel-syncs mymaster 1
Deployment guidance
  • Run three or more Sentinels across separate hosts or zones.
  • Set quorum to a majority so at least that many Sentinels must agree.
  • Avoid co-locating Sentinels with the master to reduce correlated failures.
Key Takeaway

Quorum prevents split-brain. Choose placement and quorum to favor reliable failover without blocking recovery.

screens.title: Sentinel vs. Cluster
screens.narratorSegment: Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve different problems and choosing between them depends on whether your goal is availability or scale. Sentinel provides high availability for a single master by monitoring, electing a new master on failure, and reconfiguring replicas. It does not shard data — the dataset remains on a single master and its replicas. Redis Cluster, on the other hand, partitions data across multiple master nodes so the dataset can exceed a single machine's memory and to increase write throughput by distributing keys. A concrete decision example: if your dataset fits in one machine and you need automatic failover, Sentinel is the simpler and appropriate choice. If your dataset surpasses single-node memory or your write throughput exceeds one server, Redis Cluster is the correct path, though it adds client redirection and operational complexity. A common misconception is expecting Sentinel to provide horizontal scaling — it does not. Another trap is adopting Cluster solely for HA; while Cluster has HA characteristics, its primary benefit is automatic sharding and scale. Choose based on dataset size, throughput needs, and operational readiness to manage a cluster.

keyIdea.title: Choose based on need
keyIdea.text: Sentinel = availability for single-master setups. Cluster = sharding and horizontal scaling for very large datasets or throughput needs.

content.html:
Comparison › Sentinel vs Cluster
Sentinel
  • Provides automatic failover for one master and its replicas.
  • Clients ask Sentinel for the current master address.
  • Does not shard data.
Cluster
  • Automatically shards data across multiple masters.
  • Provides high availability for each shard with replicas.
  • Clients are redirected to the correct node for a key.
Key Takeaway

Use Sentinel for availability in single-master setups; use Cluster when you need sharding and horizontal scale. They solve complementary but distinct problems.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: RDB Backup & Restore
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough rehearses a full RDB backup and restore cycle so you know each command and verification step. First, add sample data using redis-cli — for example set a user key, add a product hash, and push events to a list. Then trigger BGSAVE to create a fresh dump. rdb. After BGSAVE completes, copy dump. rdb to a separate location. Next simulate data loss by running FLUSHALL, confirming keys return nil. Stop Redis, place the backup dump. rdb into Redis's dir, restart the server, and verify the keys reappear. A key learning point is to watch for BGSAVE completion; copying before it finishes yields an older snapshot. A misconception is believing FLUSHALL will be recoverable without a backup; it is not unless you have a recent persistence file. After practicing, you should be able to run these steps confidently and understand where timing and file placement matter. Try this in a sandbox environment and record timings for each step so you can plan production maintenance windows. keyIdea.text: Execute BGSAVE, copy dump.rdb off-server, FLUSHALL to simulate loss, then restore and verify data.

content.html:
Hands-on › RDB Lab
Starter commands
# Add sample data
redis-cli SET user:1:name "Alice"
redis-cli HSET product:101 name "Laptop" price 1200 stock 50
redis-cli LPUSH log:events "Server started" "User logged in"

# Trigger snapshot
redis-cli BGSAVE

# After completion, copy dump file
cp /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb /tmp/redis_backup/dump.rdb

# Simulate data loss
redis-cli FLUSHALL
redis-cli GET user:1:name  # should return nil

# Stop, restore, start
systemctl stop redis
cp /tmp/redis_backup/dump.rdb /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb
systemctl start redis
redis-cli GET user:1:name  # should return Alice
Example scenario

Run the sequence in a VM. Record how long BGSAVE, copy, and restart take so you know expected restore time in production.

Key Takeaway

Practice the full cycle in staging. A backup is only valuable if you can restore it reliably and quickly enough for your service level objectives.

screens.title: Best Practices for Data Safety & Continuous Operation
screens.narratorSegment: To keep Redis safe in production, follow a set of complementary best practices rather than relying on a single technique. Automate backups of both RDB and AOF according to your recovery objectives, and store them off-site with timestamped filenames. Regularly test restores in a non-production environment to prove your backups are usable and to measure restore time. Monitor disk usage and persistence metrics so AOF growth or snapshot frequency does not unexpectedly exhaust space. Deploy Sentinels across multiple hosts and set an appropriate quorum to ensure reliable failover without enabling split-brain. Keep replicas even if you do not run Sentinel, so you can perform manual failover and reduce recovery time. Finally, plan capacity—AOF files can grow, and snapshots need disk space; ensure retention and rotation policies are in place. A frequent misconception is that nightly backups are sufficient for every workload; choose frequency based on acceptable data-loss windows. Combine these practices into runbooks and verify them regularly so your Redis service remains both safe and available. Run scheduled BGSAVE/BGREWRITEAOF and copy files off-site with timestamps for versioning and recovery selection.

Regularly restore backups in staging to confirm integrity and measure restore time for planning maintenance windows.

Monitor & Plan Capacity

Track AOF growth and disk usage; ensure retention and rotation to prevent full disks and failed persistence.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Backups & HA
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential concepts to remember as you apply these practices. Backup means creating copies of persistence files to protect against data loss — for Redis these are typically dump. rdb for snapshots and appendonly. aof for the write-log. Restore is the process of recovering data by placing those files in the Redis data directory and restarting the server. High Availability is the system property of remaining operational despite failures; Redis Sentinel helps achieve HA through monitoring and automated failover. These short definitions should guide your runbooks: back up regularly, test your restores, and use Sentinel to reduce downtime. As a quick reflection, ask yourself which persistence mode best matches your recovery point objective and how you will validate restores in staging before applying the same steps in production.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will make your Redis deployments resilient through practical backup, restore, and high availability patterns. You will learn how to produce consistent backups from both snapshot (RDB) and append-only (AOF) persistence, how to verify and restore those backups, and why each persistence mode matters for recovery timelines. We will then introduce Redis Sentinel and explain how it monitors Redis instances, elects leaders during failures, and provides a configuration endpoint clients can query so they don't hardcode master addresses. I will also briefly compare Sentinel with Redis Cluster to clarify when you need sharding versus when you need failover only. A concrete example you will use in the hands-on activity is creating an RDB snapshot with BGSAVE, copying the resulting dump file off-server, simulating data loss, and restoring from that file. A common misconception is thinking backups alone prevent downtime; they protect data but not availability. Sentinel addresses availability by promoting replicas automatically. By the end of this chapter you will have clear, repeatable steps to back up and restore, a working mental model for Sentinel failover, and guidance on when to consider the added complexity of a Redis Cluster.

These objectives define the hands-on and conceptual skills you'll build. First, you will develop practical strategies for backing up Redis data using both RDB snapshots and the append-only AOF file. That means learning the commands to create consistent backups, when to compact AOF, and where to store files off-server. Second, you will perform restores from RDB and AOF files so you understand the exact stop, replace, and restart sequence and how to verify a successful recovery. Third, you will understand Redis Sentinel: how it monitors instances, sends notifications, and performs automatic failover when necessary. The narration will show how Sentinels agree by quorum and how they elect a leader for failover. Fourth, you will learn how to explain Sentinel’s role as a configuration provider so clients can discover the current master address instead of hardcoding it. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue you can use to remember the steps, and every objective links to a verified competency milestone you can test in a sandbox. Practicing these goals will prepare you to keep Redis data safe, to restore quickly when problems occur, and to reduce unplanned downtime through automated failover.

We continue with four more competencies that will round out your operational readiness. First, you will practice testing restores in a non-production environment so you can trust your backups; this includes simulating data loss and verifying that keys reappear after recovery. Second, you will learn to plan backup frequency and off-site storage to reduce exposure to data loss, and you will adopt simple naming and timestamping conventions so you can select the right backup when restoring. Third, you will identify best practices for monitoring Redis persistence and disk usage so you do not run out of space for large AOF files. Fourth, you will learn the operational requirement to run multiple Sentinels across separate hosts to avoid Sentinel being a single point of failure, and how quorum reduces risk of split-brain. Each objective includes a short two-sentence task and a mnemonic to help you remember the order of operations. Practicing these objectives will make your backups trustworthy, restores verifiable, and your Sentinel deployment more resilient.

Start by understanding the two persistence modes available in Redis because your backup strategy depends on them. RDB produces point-in-time snapshots as a single binary file named dump. rdb; it is efficient for periodic, compressed backups and for fast startup because loading a single snapshot is quick. AOF records every write operation and can provide a more up-to-date recovery point, but AOF files are larger and require replay on restart. For a concrete example, imagine a shopping cart service: using RDB with regular snapshots gives you a reasonable recovery if you can tolerate up to a snapshot interval of data loss, while enabling AOF reduces that potential loss to the time between writes and the last AOF flush. A common misconception is that one persistence mode is always enough; many production deployments enable both to trade a quick restore with snapshots and a finer-grained recovery with AOF. When you plan backups, consider restore time, acceptable data-loss window, disk usage, and startup performance. As you work through the hands-on activity, pick the mode that matches your recovery point objective and validate it with a test restore so you can trust the recovery SLA.

Backing up an RDB snapshot is a simple, repeatable process that you should automate. First, confirm RDB persistence is enabled in redis. conf via the save directives; these settings decide when Redis creates periodic snapshots. Second, trigger an immediate snapshot with BGSAVE so the server creates a fresh dump without blocking clients. Third, wait for the BGSAVE completion message or check the last save time, then locate the dump. rdb file in the configured dir and dbfilename locations. Fourth, copy that file to an off-server location such as cloud storage or a separate backup host, and add a timestamp to the filename to keep versions. For example, after running BGSAVE you might run a command to copy dump. rdb to /tmp/redis_backup/dump-2023-07-01. rdb. A common mistake is copying the file before BGSAVE finishes, which yields an old snapshot; always confirm completion. Another trap is keeping backups on the same disk — off-site copies are essential. As a practice, automate BGSAVE triggers and file transfer and make sure your restore process is tested periodically so backups are not just created, but also usable when you need them.

Restoring from an RDB file is straightforward but must be done carefully to avoid corruption or partial restores. The safe sequence is: stop the Redis server cleanly so it does not overwrite or conflict with the file you will restore; place your validated dump. rdb into the Redis dir configured in redis. conf; then restart the Redis server so it will load the snapshot at startup. For example, after copying your backup dump into the configured directory, run the server start command and then verify keys using redis-cli GET or HGET. A common mistake is attempting to replace the file while Redis is running, which can cause the running process to overwrite the file or encounter inconsistent state. Another misconception is that restores are instant — loading a large snapshot can take time and you should monitor server logs for completion. Always practice the restore in a staging environment to confirm timelines and the correctness of your backup selection. Finally, consider locking or versioning the dir during restore so multiple processes do not interfere with the operation. Restoring from an RDB Backup means stop redis, replace dump.rdb in the configured dir, restart, and verify with commands in redis-cli.. In practical terms, stop redis, replace dump.rdb, and restart to recover state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AOF backups require additional care because the file records every write and can grow quickly. First, enable AOF by setting appendonly yes in redis. conf and confirm the appendfilename and dir settings. Second, trigger BGREWRITEAOF to compact the AOF into a smaller, optimized file that removes redundant commands; BGREWRITEAOF runs in the background and produces a compacted appendonly. aof. Third, after BGREWRITEAOF completes, copy the resulting appendonly. aof to a safe off-server location, applying timestamps so you can choose the correct recovery point. A concrete example: after a large ingestion job, run BGREWRITEAOF then copy appendonly. aof to cloud storage. A common mistake is copying the AOF before compaction, which produces larger files and slower restores. Also avoid keeping backups on the same disk. Finally, remember that restoring from AOF involves replaying commands during startup, which can take additional time proportional to the file size; plan restore windows accordingly and test them in staging. Creating and Compacting an AOF Backup means enable appendonly, run bgrewriteaof to compact, and copy appendonly.aof off-server; expect longer replay time on restore.. In practical terms, enable aof, run bgrewriteaof, and copy the appendonly.aof file off-server.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Restoring from AOF differs from RDB because Redis will replay the logged operations to rebuild the dataset. The safe restore sequence is: stop the Redis server, place the appendonly. aof file into the configured dir with the correct appendfilename, and restart Redis so it can read and replay the commands. During restart Redis will process each entry; for large AOF files this can take time proportional to the command count. A concrete scenario: you compacted an AOF, copied it off-site, and now need to restore after data loss. You would stop Redis, replace appendonly. aof, restart, and then monitor logs for replay completion before sending production traffic. A misconception is thinking AOF restores are faster than RDB; in many cases a compacted AOF can be larger than RDB and will take longer because it has to execute commands. Always test your AOF restore process to understand time requirements and any command semantics that might change during replay. Restoring from an AOF Backup means aof replays commands during startup. expect longer startup times and test restores to measure them.. In practical terms, stop redis, place appendonly.aof, restart and let aof replay rebuild state.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redis Sentinel is a small distributed system that provides high availability for a Redis deployment. Its responsibilities are fourfold: continuous monitoring of master and replica instances, notification to operators or monitoring systems when anomalies are detected, automatic failover to promote a replica to master when a master is unavailable, and serving as a configuration provider that clients can query for the current master address. For example, if a master becomes unresponsive, Sentinels mark it subjectively down and then, through a quorum of Sentinels, mark it objectively down. Once the quorum agrees, they elect a leader Sentinel to orchestrate failover: choose the best replica, promote it, reconfigure remaining replicas to follow the new master, and inform clients. A common misconception is that Sentinel replaces backups: it does not. Sentinel reduces downtime by automating role changes but does not undo data loss that occurred before backups. Understanding Sentinel’s roles clarifies why production systems usually combine backups for data safety and Sentinel for availability. Redis Sentinel: Purpose and Core Functions means sentinel monitors, notifies, performs failover, and tells clients which node is master — but it is not a backup system.. In practical terms, monitoring, notification, automatic failover, and configuration provider.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A healthy Sentinel deployment uses multiple Sentinel processes on separate hosts and a quorum-based decision to avoid split-brain. The sentinel. conf includes a monitor line that names the master and sets the quorum number — for example, sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2 requires at least two Sentinels to agree a master is down before failover. Sentinels first detect outages subjectively; then when enough Sentinels report the same condition, the master becomes objectively down and a leader is elected to manage failover. Running at least three Sentinels ensures no single Sentinel can unilaterally decide failure and allows a majority to form. A common operational pitfall is collocating Sentinels with the master as they then risk being unavailable during the same outage; place Sentinels on separate hosts or availability zones. Another misconception is that a higher quorum is always safer; too high a quorum can prevent failover if Sentinels are temporarily partitioned. Balance quorum and placement for reliable failover. Practice reviewing sentinel. conf and simulating failover in a staging environment to validate your choices. Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve different problems and choosing between them depends on whether your goal is availability or scale. Sentinel provides high availability for a single master by monitoring, electing a new master on failure, and reconfiguring replicas. It does not shard data — the dataset remains on a single master and its replicas. Redis Cluster, on the other hand, partitions data across multiple master nodes so the dataset can exceed a single machine's memory and to increase write throughput by distributing keys. A concrete decision example: if your dataset fits in one machine and you need automatic failover, Sentinel is the simpler and appropriate choice. If your dataset surpasses single-node memory or your write throughput exceeds one server, Redis Cluster is the correct path, though it adds client redirection and operational complexity. A common misconception is expecting Sentinel to provide horizontal scaling — it does not. Another trap is adopting Cluster solely for HA; while Cluster has HA characteristics, its primary benefit is automatic sharding and scale. Choose based on dataset size, throughput needs, and operational readiness to manage a cluster.

This hands-on walkthrough rehearses a full RDB backup and restore cycle so you know each command and verification step. First, add sample data using redis-cli — for example set a user key, add a product hash, and push events to a list. Then trigger BGSAVE to create a fresh dump. rdb. After BGSAVE completes, copy dump. rdb to a separate location. Next simulate data loss by running FLUSHALL, confirming keys return nil. Stop Redis, place the backup dump. rdb into Redis's dir, restart the server, and verify the keys reappear. A key learning point is to watch for BGSAVE completion; copying before it finishes yields an older snapshot. A misconception is believing FLUSHALL will be recoverable without a backup; it is not unless you have a recent persistence file. To keep Redis safe in production, follow a set of complementary best practices rather than relying on a single technique. Automate backups of both RDB and AOF according to your recovery objectives, and store them off-site with timestamped filenames. Regularly test restores in a non-production environment to prove your backups are usable and to measure restore time. Monitor disk usage and persistence metrics so AOF growth or snapshot frequency does not unexpectedly exhaust space. Deploy Sentinels across multiple hosts and set an appropriate quorum to ensure reliable failover without enabling split-brain. Keep replicas even if you do not run Sentinel, so you can perform manual failover and reduce recovery time. Finally, plan capacity—AOF files can grow, and snapshots need disk space; ensure retention and rotation policies are in place. A frequent misconception is that nightly backups are sufficient for every workload; choose frequency based on acceptable data-loss windows. Combine these practices into runbooks and verify them regularly so your Redis service remains both safe and available. Here are the essential concepts to remember as you apply these practices. Backup means creating copies of persistence files to protect against data loss — for Redis these are typically dump. rdb for snapshots and appendonly. aof for the write-log. Restore is the process of recovering data by placing those files in the Redis data directory and restarting the server. High Availability is the system property of remaining operational despite failures; Redis Sentinel helps achieve HA through monitoring and automated failover. These short definitions should guide your runbooks: back up regularly, test your restores, and use Sentinel to reduce downtime. As a quick reflection, ask yourself which persistence mode best matches your recovery point objective and how you will validate restores in staging before applying the same steps in production.

A few operational terms you will use in conversations and runbooks: Redis Sentinel performs monitoring and automatic failover, electing leaders through a quorum of Sentinels so a majority decides on failover actions. Failover is the process of switching to a replica when the master is down. Quorum is the minimum number of Sentinels that must agree on a master's failure, which prevents split-brain. Redis Cluster is the solution for automatic sharding and horizontal scaling across multiple masters; clients are redirected to the correct node for a key. Keep these concise definitions handy when designing architecture: Sentinel for availability in single-shard setups, Cluster for sharding and scale. As you apply these ideas, remember to combine them with backups since HA prevents downtime but does not replace data backups.
